text:
A: Hello, Harriet? Karim. Can you hear me all right?
B: Hi, yeah. Sorry, I'm a bit quiet, I think. Is that okay?
A: Perfect. Don't worry, I'm loud enough for both of us. How's it going so far?
B: Erm, okay. It's a bit strange, isn't it, just talking to strangers for three minutes.
A: It is. I actually like it, though. You get the good bits without the small talk. So, I'm going to guess. You're surrounded by books, you look like you've got a massive to-do list. Student?
B: [laughs] Yeah, that's fair. Final year history at Queen Mary. And yes, the to-do list is massive.
A: History! What's your thing?
B: I'm doing a dissertation on women's lodging houses in Victorian East London. So, sort of, where single women stayed if they didn't have family. Who ran them, what the rules were, that kind of thing.
A: Okay, that's brilliant. Were they decent places, or grim?
B: Mostly grim, I think. Some of the charity ones were really strict, like, curfews and prayers and you'd get chucked out for coming back drunk. But they were also the only way some women could be, I don't know, independent at all. If that makes sense.
A: No, it does. Safety but with somebody watching you. That's every immigrant family as well, to be honest. We came from Basra when I was fourteen, a year in Jordan first, and the first place we stayed in Birmingham, there was an old lady downstairs who knew everything everyone did.
B: Oh, wow. Was that hard? Moving at fourteen?
A: At the time I thought it was an adventure. Now I've got a fifteen-year-old and I think, if I moved him tomorrow, he'd never forgive me. So I probably didn't understand what my parents were carrying.
B: Yeah. I think you only get that later.
A: How far through are you, the dissertation?
B: Erm. Honestly? About a third, maybe less. It's due in May. I've had an extension already. I'm just really bad at starting. I'll read for hours and not write anything.
A: Mate, I have four thousand emails in my inbox. I'm the last person to judge you. But reading for hours, that's not nothing. That's the bit that makes it good.
B: That's kind. I'm not sure my supervisor sees it that way.
A: Supervisors never do. What are you reading, apart from Victorian landladies?
B: Erm, three novels at once, which is a problem. A Sarah Waters, an Elizabeth Strout and a Barbara Pym I found at the shop for two pounds. First edition.
A: Two pounds! See, I'm the same, three on the go, never finish. I'm halfway through a translated Turkish one at the moment, and a history of Birmingham's canals. I'm still angry they knocked down the old Central Library, by the way, that was a beautiful ugly building.
B: [laughs] Beautiful ugly. I like that. I go to the William Morris Gallery a lot, because it's round the corner. He'd probably have hated it, though, wouldn't he.
A: He'd have written a very long letter about it. Is the gallery good?
B: It's lovely. It's free and it's quiet, and there's a garden. I sometimes go there instead of working.
A: That's research, that. I'm putting it on my list. Next time I'm in London I'll go and
